Lecture 20

Indented contours, principal values and branch cuts

Lecture objectives

We find the limits of small-arc integrals, compare ordinary and principal-value integrals, and evaluate principal values by indented paths. We derive Si⁡(∞)=π/2\Si(\infty)=\pi/2Si(∞)=π/2 and integrate over the positive half-axis with a keyhole path around a branch cut.

Lecture 19 closed the segment [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] with a semicircle and evaluated real integrals by residues, for integrands without singular points on the real axis. In this lecture the integrand may have simple poles on the real axis. The path then passes these points on small semicircles, and the real integral becomes a principal value in the sense of Lecture 17. In this way we compute the sine integral at infinity. Finally we integrate a power xα−1x^{\alpha-1}xα−1 times a rational function over the positive half-axis. The power is a branch with a cut along that half-axis, and the path runs along the two sides of the cut. The lecture reads in three stages: arcs and principal values (Sections 20.1–20.2), indented paths with the sine integral and two poles on the line (Sections 20.3–20.5), and keyhole paths (Section 20.6).

20.2 Ordinary and principal-value integrals

On the line we also cut off symmetrically at infinity, as in the integrals ∫−RR\int_{-R}^R∫−RR​ of Lecture 19.

Summary

An integral over the line through a simple pole exists only as a principal value. Passing each real simple pole on a small semicircle shows that it contributes half of what an enclosed pole contributes, whichever side the indentation takes. For a weighted integral over the positive half-axis the branch of zα−1z^{\alpha-1}zα−1 is fixed with its cut along that half-axis. The two banks then carry the factors 111 and e2πiα,\ee^{2\pi\iu\alpha}e2πiα, and the keyhole path turns the integral into a sum of residues.

  • Small arcs: if (z−z0)f(z)→β,(z-z_0)f(z)\to\beta(z−z0​)f(z)→β, then ∫Aε(z0;θ1,θ2)f ⁣dz→i(θ2−θ1)β;\int_{A_\varepsilon(z_0;\theta_1,\theta_2)}f\dd z\to\iu(\theta_2-\theta_1)\beta∫Aε​(z0​;θ1​,θ2​)​fdz→i(θ2​−θ1​)β; at a simple pole β=Res⁡z=z0f;\beta=\Res_{z=z_0}fβ=Resz=z0​​f; the clockwise upper-semicircle integral of 1/z21/z^21/z2 is −2/ε-2/\varepsilon−2/ε and diverges.

  • Principal values: an ordinary improper integral equals its principal value; the converse fails; β/(x−x0)\beta/(x-x_0)β/(x−x0​) with β≠0\beta\ne0β=0 has only a principal value at x0.x_0x0​.

  • Indentation: pv⁡∫eikxP/Q ⁣dx=2πi∑Im⁡zj>0Res⁡+πi∑mRes⁡z=xm\pv\int\ee^{\iu kx}P/Q\dd x=2\pi\iu\sum_{\Im z_j>0}\Res+\pi\iu\sum_m\Res_{z=x_m}pv∫eikxP/Qdx=2πi∑Imzj​>0​Res+πi∑m​Resz=xm​​ for simple real zeros xmx_mxm​ of Q,QQ, with k>0k>0k>0 and deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+1,\deg Q\ge\deg P+1degQ≥degP+1, or k=0k=0k=0 and deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2.\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2.

  • Sine integral: Si⁡(∞)=∫0∞sin⁡x ⁣dx/x=π/2;\Si(\infty)=\int_0^\infty\sin x\dd x/x=\pi/2Si(∞)=∫0∞​sinxdx/x=π/2; the integral does not converge absolutely.

  • Keyhole: for 0<α<1,0<\alpha<10<α<1, deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+1\deg Q\ge\deg P+1degQ≥degP+1 and Q≠0Q\ne0Q=0 on [0,∞),[0,\infty)[0,∞), ∫0∞xα−1P/Q ⁣dx=2πi(1−e2πiα)−1∑jRes⁡(zα−1P/Q)\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}P/Q\dd x=2\pi\iu(1-\ee^{2\pi\iu\alpha})^{-1}\sum_j\Res(z^{\alpha-1}P/Q)∫0∞​xα−1P/Qdx=2πi(1−e2πiα)−1∑j​Res(zα−1P/Q) with 0<arg⁡z<2π;0<\arg z<2\pi0<argz<2π; for example ∫0∞xα−1 ⁣dx/(1+x)=π/sin⁡(πα).\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}\dd x/(1+x)=\pi/\sin(\pi\alpha)∫0∞​xα−1dx/(1+x)=π/sin(πα).

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. A function has a simple pole at zero with residue 222. A small upper semicircle runs from −ε-\varepsilon−ε to +ε+\varepsilon+ε. Find the imaginary part of the limiting arc integral as ε→0+\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+. Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Write the starting and ending angles before applying the small-arc formula.

The singular term is 2/z2/z2/z. With z=εeiθz=\varepsilon\ee^{\iu\theta}z=εeiθ it contributes 2i ⁣dθ2\iu\dd\theta2idθ to the integral, and the bounded remainder has a vanishing integral. The angle decreases from π\piπ to 000, giving −2πi-2\pi\iu−2πi. The imaginary part is −2π-2\pi−2π.

2. In what sense does the integral of 1/x1/x1/x over [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] exist?

Hint. Compare separate one-sided limits with a shared symmetric exclusion around zero.

The left and right integrals diverge separately with opposite signs, so the ordinary improper integral fails. With a common cutoff ε\varepsilonε their logarithmic terms cancel at every cutoff, giving principal value zero. Oddness enforces that cancellation only for the symmetric cutoff. Separate divergence cannot rule out that principal value.

3. What is pv⁡∫−∞∞(x+1)/[x(x2+1)] ⁣dx\pv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x+1)/[x(x^2+1)]\dd xpv∫−∞∞​(x+1)/[x(x2+1)]dx, using a symmetric exclusion at zero?

Hint. Close above and exclude the real pole by a clockwise small arc. Which residue remains inside?

The upper pole at i\iui has residue −(1+i)/2-(1+\iu)/2−(1+i)/2, so the closed integral is π−πi\pi-\pi\iuπ−πi. The large arc vanishes by quadratic decay. The real pole has residue 111 and the clockwise indentation contributes −πi-\pi\iu−πi. Subtracting it gives π\piπ. Omitting the indentation leaves π−πi\pi-\pi\iuπ−πi, and reversing its sign gives π−2πi\pi-2\pi\iuπ−2πi. The negative real answer reverses the sign of the integral of the even term 1/(x2+1)1/(x^2+1)1/(x2+1), since the odd term has principal value zero.

4. In a keyhole contour use z−2/3z^{-2/3}z−2/3 with 0<arg⁡z<2π0<\arg z<2\pi0<argz<2π. For the integrand z−2/3h(z)z^{-2/3}h(z)z−2/3h(z) the upper bank contributes a nonzero value III. The factor hhh has the same boundary values on both banks. What is the lower bank’s contribution on the positively oriented path, for the same two radial endpoints?

Hint. Check both the argument on the lower bank and its direction of traversal.

The argument is zero on the upper bank in the limit and 2π2\pi2π on the lower bank. The lower value therefore has factor e−4πi/3=e2πi/3\ee^{-4\pi\iu/3}=\ee^{2\pi\iu/3}e−4πi/3=e2πi/3 relative to the upper one. The lower bank runs from the outer radius to the inner radius, supplying a minus sign. Keeping the phase alone loses the direction. Keeping the minus sign alone loses the phase, and using its conjugate reverses the argument change.
